title: CPU baseline matmul throughput
status: Measured on DE1-SoC · ARM Cortex-A9 · 2 threads, NEON SIMD kernel, 32×32 tiling
description:
CPU baseline for an N×N int8 matmul, measured with matmul_baseline_mt (tile 32, 2 threads, NEON kernel) on the DE1-SoC's dual-core ARM Cortex-A9. The linked text file has the raw output, every number and the full calculation.

Optimization setup:
- Tiling: 32×32 tiles.
- 2 threads: one per Cortex-A9 core. The rows of C are split between the threads, which never need to synchronise.
- SIMD NEON kernel: NEON instructions process 16 int8 values per 128-bit register. The kernel computes 4 output columns at once with 4 independent accumulators.
- Compiled with gcc -O3 -mcpu=cortex-a9 -mfpu=neon.

How GOP/s is calculated: GOP/s = 2 × N³ / time.
- An N×N by N×N matmul has N² outputs, and each output is a dot product of length N, so it does N³ multiply-accumulates (MACs).
- Each MAC counts as 2 operations (one multiply and one add), so the total is 2 × N³ operations.
- Dividing by the measured time in seconds gives operations per second; dividing by 10⁹ gives GOP/s.
- Example, N = 128: 2 × 128³ = 4,194,304 operations in 689.52 µs = 4,194,304 / 0.00068952 s = 6.083 × 10⁹ operations per second = 6.083 GOP/s.

title: Matmul performance analysis (summary) — stale, 90 MHz build
status: Stale · old 90 MHz build · full write-up on GitHub
description:
Stale: this analysis is from the old 90 MHz build. The accelerator now runs at 75 MHz; current numbers are in "Matmul throughput by tile size (75 MHz)".

Summary of PERF_ANALYSIS.md for the 16×16 int8 weight-stationary systolic array at 90 MHz on the DE1-SoC. Full write-up in the matmul-accel repo (link above).

Main conclusion: performance is bound by the software tiling scheme. Each matmul the hardware runs multiplies a tk×tn slab of W by a tn×tm slab of X into a tk×tm output patch. A bigger output patch gets more MACs from each byte sent over the bridge (density), so the same problem needs fewer matmuls and fewer bytes.

- A 256×256 matmul tiled into 128×128 output tiles runs at the same speed as a single 128×128 matmul: same tile shape, density and utilization. Tiling it as one 256×256 output (W in 256×64 strips, X in 64×256 strips) halves the matmul count and roughly doubles throughput.
- A 128×128 matmul is capped at 64 MAC/B because a tile cannot be larger than the matrix. 256×256 reaches 128 MAC/B, the limit set by the 64 KB output canvas, so 512×512 plateaus at the same density.
- Peak compute is 46.1 GOP/s (2 ops × 256 PEs × 90 MHz). Best measured compute-only throughput is 40.15 GOP/s, about 87% of peak.
- The gap comes from 16 head and 16 tail cycles per weight block: utilization = tm / (tm + 32), 80% at tm = 128 and 88.9% at tm = 256. Overlapping the next block's head with the previous block's tail would bring utilization close to 100%; that needs the output path to hold two blocks in flight.

title: Matmul throughput by tile size (75 MHz)
description:
One matmul per row: a tk×tn weight block times a tn×tm input block, DMA both ways, with bias off and on.
Compute GOP/s counts array compute only. End-to-end GOP/s also includes the input DMA, the bias stage and the output DMA.

title: MNN / TinyViT FPGA integration report
status: Functional integration demonstrated · full report on GitHub
description: Full TinyViT inference completed on the DE1-SoC with the selected Q × Kᵀ attention MatMul (/layers.3/blocks.1/attn/MatMul_output_0) offloaded to the FPGA; the rest of the model runs on the CPU. Each of 10 heads multiplies a 49 × 32 Q matrix by a 32 × 49 transposed K matrix. Software splits this into 16 × 16 × 16 FPGA jobs, pads the final row and column tiles, and accumulates the two reduction tiles on the CPU. Both synthetic inputs completed and six physical matrix tests passed. The compute-share estimate compares useful MACs for this operation with Microsoft's published TinyViT-21M at 224 × 224; it is not a measured operation count for the deployed MNN model.
